rejections.detail: The returned book allocated 8% to "IUSX", described in its own thesis as the "iShares MSCI USA Dividend ETF". There is no such listing; the price source answers "No data found, symbol may be delisted". Nothing downstream can price it, and the tracker's refuse-to-score guard caught it and declined to write any round-3 artifact at all rather than mark the leg at par.
rejections.handling: Refused whole, per the protocol's rule that a rejected book means the manager's prior book stands. The leg was deliberately NOT dropped and the remaining weights were NOT rescaled: that would be the desk rewriting a manager's decision into one it never made, and it would break weights+cash=100. The manager was not given a second attempt, because no other manager got one. Its Round 2 return was unaffected and was accepted.
rejections.fix: tracker/desk_apply.py now resolves every symbol in an incoming book against the price source before accepting it, so an unexecutable book is refused at the desk in the same pass as the hard rules instead of halting the whole round's scoring days later.

decisions.reason:
The leg I am being asked to reconsider is three sessions old (filled 2026-09-16) and it was built for exactly the regime that has since been confirmed, so trading again now would be churn dressed up as work. What I checked before deciding: the FOMC did raise the target range 25bp to 3.75-4.00% on 9/16 - unanimous 12-0, first hike since 2023, explicitly justified by elevated inflation, with the median year-end funds rate marked up to 4.1%. The long end sold off with it rather than rallying: the 10y closed 5.01% on 9/18 against 4.79% at the start of September, with 2s at 4.10%, so the curve bear-steepened roughly 90bp while the Fed was tightening. That is a hot-nominal-growth, rising-discount-rate world, and it is the precise argument for owning high-ROIC net-cash franchises whose earnings reprice with nominal spend and who EARN the 4-5% on their own balance sheets instead of paying it. It is an argument against levered, long-payback, cash-burning duration. My five legs are the first thing and own none of the second.

Leg by leg, nothing broke. NVDA marks +3.91% at 222.27 on a 28x trailing multiple with Huang guiding to roughly double the chips shipped next year - that is a growth-adjusted multiple below the index's 25x, not a bubble leg. TSM marks +4.06% at 434.67 after a record NT$514.8bn August and with 2nm entering phones; it is the toll booth rather than the bet on any single accelerator winner, which is why it sits alongside NVDA rather than being crowded out by it. GOOGL, my largest weight at 24%, marks +1.95% and got the single best piece of news in the window: the unsealed adtech remedy is interoperability and publisher data sharing, not divestiture, which removes the tail risk that was the main reason to underweight it - and it still trades at 17.5x with revenue +20%. META marks -1.12% and is the cheapest thing I own at 20.6x forward while still -14% YTD; Muse topping the App Store and the Stilla.ai agent deal are early evidence the capex is starting to produce monetizable product, and I am not selling a laggard into the first sign the thesis is turning. V marks -0.71%, which is what ballast is supposed to do in a three-day window - it is my only non-AI leg and its whole job is to convert elevated inflation into fee revenue.

The one honest criticism of this book is concentration: 68% of gross sits in a single AI-complex factor, and if capex sentiment cracks four of my five legs fall together. I have decided to keep that exposure rather than diversify it away, because the 16% cash buffer plus stops at -14% to -20% and take-profits on the two hottest legs already define my loss, and because diluting into lower-ROIC non-tech compounders purely for correlation cosmetics would violate the mandate that picked these names in the first place. Re-trading would also reset every stop to a new, higher entry basis and silently loosen my downside - a real cost on top of the 4-8bp of commission and SEC fees a full replacement burns. NAV is +4.83% against SPY +2.73% on 84% gross; the position is working, the reason it was working has just been confirmed by the Fed and the tape, and the correct action when your thesis is confirmed is to let it run, not to trade on top of it.

Two things changed since 2026-09-16. First, the event I de-risked for is behind me: the Fed delivered the 25bp hike on 09-16, equities rebounded into it (SPY 761.69, ~2% off the high; IWM +21% YTD and beating SPY; S&P earnings running +51%), and I spent that rally earning 4% on 30% of the book. The de-risk was right on process and wrong on P&L - I am +2.57% versus SPY +2.73% while carrying single-name small-cap risk on only 70% of capital. That is the worst of both worlds and I am fixing it by taking gross to 88%. Second, and this is the part that reshapes the book rather than just resizing it: the 10-year has briefly traded through 5% for the first time since 2023, the 30-year is at its highest since 2007, and WTI is above $100 on the attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline. That is not a backdrop where I want my two biggest risk budgets in the most duration-sensitive things I own. So the re-risk is deliberately asymmetric: I add to profitable, fast-compounding names with visible near-term catalysts and I cut the legs whose entire case is multiple expansion. GTLB goes to zero - 23% revenue growth, still loss-making, 56x forward, already +46% in three months, only ~12% to consensus target and no catalyst until December; in a 5%-yield regime that is the clearest sell in the book. XBI is halved from 19% to 12%: it was my largest weight and my lowest-conviction leg (156 equal-weighted holdings and the tightest stop I set, which tells me I never really believed it), it is +68% over a year and testing the 2021 high at $174.79, and equal-weight biotech is the purest long-duration asset in the small/mid universe exactly as the long end breaks 5%. The freed capital goes to HOOD, NU, ALAB and new position CRDO. I also fixed the sizing inversion: my two best legs (HOOD +14.8%, ALAB +12.7% in two sessions) were sized 15% and 9% while my flattest leg was 19%. Conviction and weight now point the same way. Cash stays at a real 12% rather than the 10% default because an oil shock plus a hiking Fed is a live tail, and every leg carries a hard stop.
decisions.strategy: Re-risked concentrated small/mid-cap growth book: gross lifted from 70% to 88% now the September FOMC event risk has passed, rotated out of unprofitable and pure-duration exposure (GTLB cut, XBI halved) into four earnings-backed compounders levered to crypto/tokenization, LatAm fintech and AI connectivity.

The ballast that lets me carry the rest of this concentration. It is also structurally the one leg that is helped rather than hurt by higher policy rates, because it earns a spread on a deposit base rather than discounting terminal value. New position, and the single cheapest growth in the book on the numbers that matter now: 24x forward earnings against 165% ttm revenue growth, versus ALAB's 54x on 100%. Fiscal 2026 revenue grew 206% to $1.34B and earnings grew 805% to $472M, and the new 224G optical transceiver line extends it up the AI-infrastructure stack. The reason it is available at 24x is that the stock fell nearly 50% from its 2026 high of $308.67 and JPMorgan and BofA trimmed targets on tempered growth expectations after the last print - but both kept positive ratings and the consensus target of $282 implies 61% upside, the widest in my book. It rose 4.5% on 09-18, so the recovery has begun rather than being hypothetical. Sized at 15% - below ALAB - because it is the more contested of the two theses and carries genuine estimate-cut risk into its next print; the 25% stop and 55% take-profit reflect a deliberately wider distribution than anything else I hold.

Cut from 19% to 12% but deliberately not to zero. The cut is a rates call: equal-weighted biotech is the longest-duration equity exposure available in small/mid-cap, and the long end just printed 5% on the 10-year and a post-2007 high on the 30-year with the Fed actively hiking. XBI is +67.9% over the past year and is now pressing the 2021 high at $174.79 after a bullish-flag breakout, which is a level that takes multiple attempts to clear and usually does not clear it while discount rates are rising. Having my largest weight in a 156-holding equal-weight index fund was also a mandate problem - that is closet indexing, not the concentrated conviction this book is paid for. What keeps 12% in place is that the sector's own cycle is independent of rates: M&A has been the driver of this year's move and large-cap pharma patent cliffs do not care about the 10-year, so a full exit would be a pure macro bet against a working idiosyncratic catalyst. The 13% stop is the tightest in the book precisely because this is the leg I am least willing to defend if the rates move keeps going.

decisions.reason: This leg (VZ 20/MO 17/C 13/BTI 10/PFE 8, 32% cash) is only 11 trading days old (entered 2026-09-08) and every leg's fundamentals are intact: no dividend has been cut or put at real risk (VZ ex-div 10/9 at $0.707, BTI ex-div 10/2 at $0.835, MO forward yield 6.39%, PFE forward yield 6.22% all confirmed still being paid), no earnings disaster has landed (VZ and BTI don't report until late Oct/Nov, PFE not until 11/3, and C's Q2 print actually raised its 2026 RoTCE outlook above 11% with a Truist Buy reiterated), and P/Es remain in the cheap 10-15x band across the book (C 14.2x, MO 14.6x, BTI 14.3x trailing/10.7x forward, PFE mid-teens). The disciplined move for a deep-value dividend book is to let a genuinely cheap, income-generating basket ride through ordinary rate-driven noise rather than churn on an 11-day sample, so I am holding the book exactly as filled, unchanged into the 2026-09-21 close.

The book is doing exactly what a long-only dividend-growth/aristocrats basket is supposed to do: +3.16% since 2026-07-17 vs SPY +2.73%, with a shallow -2.74% max drawdown and no leg anywhere near its stop. The one macro wrinkle is that the Sep 16 FOMC actually hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00% on 'elevated' inflation rather than cutting, which is a headwind for equity multiples broadly, but it's precisely the environment (inflation persistence, capital rotating toward cash-generative, pricing-power names) where a dividend-aristocrats/staples-plus-energy-hedge book is the right posture, not the wrong one -- CVX's energy hedge is doing its intended job (+12.8% leg P&L) against that inflation backdrop. Nothing in this sweep constitutes a thesis-breaking catalyst for any of the eight holdings, and the mandate is explicitly a low-turnover, buy-and-hold dividend-growth strategy -- forcing a rebalance here would just pay the desk's transaction costs to arrive back at a substantially similar book. Holding preserves the compounding dividend stream, keeps the small energy hedge in place while oil-supply risk is live, and avoids churn with no offsetting information edge.

Holding preserves the intact thesis and avoids paying churn costs on a book that has not generated a valid signal to act on.

For a beta-matched, nine-sector, thirteen-name residual book that is comfortably inside one sigma over three days; treating it as evidence would be confusing a weekly mark with a signal. Second, and more concretely, I would be rescreening off 2026-09-18 closes, and 2026-09-18 was September quadruple witching with roughly $6tn of options exposure expiring plus quarterly index rebalancing. Those closes carry pin and roll distortion in exactly the cross-sectional dimension my screen reads - residual vol and pairwise residual correlation - and a meaningful share of Friday's single-name dispersion typically reverses in the following week. Rebuilding a residual-correlation screen on witching prints is the single worst day of the quarter to do it. Third, the 2026 factor backdrop still argues for the structure as built: equal-weight has beaten cap-weight by about five points year to date and leadership has broadened into financials, industrials and healthcare, so a diversified nine-sector long basket financed by a cap-weighted SPY short is long the factor that has been paying, and the last two sessions' mega-cap tech bounce is the counter-move a dispersion book is supposed to sit through rather than chase. Fourth, the design premise is intact: the offsetting macro loadings were chosen for a rate-up world and we now have an explicit restarting hiking cycle, which is the regime CME and GPN were sized for, and the basket still holds no AI-capex names, so my residual is stock selection rather than a bet on the AI complex. Fifth, the one leg whose thesis the hiking cycle genuinely degrades is CHTR: 4.4x net debt/EBITDA, 2.4x interest cover, a $90bn+ stack being refinanced at 7%+ coupons after the Liberty Broadband and Cox closes, and it is already my worst mark at -5.06%. But it is 3.2% of the book with a -20% stop, so the entire remaining downside I am underwriting there is about 48bps of NAV, and the only way this format lets me remove it is to replace all fourteen legs - repricing the other twelve longs and the SPY short at Monday's close, resetting every stop reference away from fills I understand, and paying spread and SEC/TAF across the whole $950 of gross. Paying a full-book turn to excise one contained 3.2% position is a bad trade. Finally, turnover discipline: this is leg 8 in nine weeks. A dispersion book earns from residual convergence that needs weeks to express, and rescreening every Monday guarantees I pay the costs of the strategy while never holding a position long enough to collect its payoff. The screen is three days old, it was built on the right information, and the correct action is to let it work.

Three things changed this week and all three argue for less risk, not more. (1) ACA is no longer a near-dated catalyst. The stockholder vote passed on 2026-09-04 (39.6m for, 66k against), but the HSR waiting period has NOT expired, and the merger agreement's outside date is 2027-06-21 with automatic extensions to 2027-09-21 and 2027-12-21 if regulatory conditions are unresolved. Q1 2027 is a goal, not a commitment. The remaining spread is 145.84 to 150.00 = 2.85%; over a 5-month close that is ~6.8% annualized and over a 9-month close it is ~3.8% - i.e. at or below cash - against a break tail worth roughly -25% to -30%. A thin-edge, fat-tail position does not deserve a third of the book, so ACA goes 33 -> 22. (2) I priced the rest of the arb complex and it is worse. LXP closed 60.81 Friday against Brookfield/CPPIB's 61.20 all-cash with a Q4 2026 target: 0.64% gross, ~2.6% annualized, below cash after 2bps each way - I am not paying fees to earn less than idle balances. WBD is the one genuinely live situation (31.00 cash, ticking fee from 2026-09-30, FCC foreign-ownership clearance 2026-09-17), but it closed 27.80 and then jumped roughly 8% after hours Friday on the WSJ settlement-talks report. My entry is the Monday close, so I would be buying the news, not the event - paying ~29.5-30.1 for ~4-7% of residual upside while Bonta, who already walked out of talks once citing bad faith, can reprice it -10% in an afternoon. Declined. (3) CRM's drift thesis has inverted and I am cutting it outright: the stock fell on a fiscal-2027 guidance raise, fell again into Dreamforce, is down ~30% YTD, and the -4.87% mark is the market telling me the revision tailwind I bought is not there. The honest conclusion of a week's research is that the event calendar is empty at a price I want, and the correct event-driven answer to an empty calendar is cash - especially with the Fed having hiked to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16, 16 of 18 dots showing at least one more hike this year, and the 10-year back above 5%. Gross exposure falls 70% -> 47%.
decisions.strategy: A deliberately de-risked event book: a right-sized CRH/Arcosa cash-merger carry, a trimmed energy leg as the supply-disruption tail, one post-earnings-drift long with confirmed upward revision breadth, a small index short against a hiking Fed, and a majority cash position because 4% cash currently out-yields the entire tight-spread merger-arb complex.

positions.thesis: CRH acquiring Arcosa for $150.00/share in all cash; stockholders approved 2026-09-04 by an overwhelming margin, financing is CRH cash plus committed debt so there is no funding risk, and the position is immune to the index beta and rate path that drives everything else in this book. What is left is purely regulatory: HSR clearance is still outstanding and CRH is the largest US aggregates producer buying a major aggregates/infrastructure player, so a second request and divestiture remedies are live possibilities, with CRH's obligation to accept remedies contractually capped. That is why the spread is 2.85% while a clean financial-buyer REIT deal like LXP trades at 0.64% - the width is payment for timeline and remedy risk, not free money. I want the carry but at carry size, so 22% rather than 33%. Take-profit at 3.0% sits just above the $150 deal price so the leg closes itself on consummation; the 8% stop is not gap protection against a break but does cap the bleed if a second request resets the market's clock toward the 2027 outside date.

The physical-supply event I bought this for is repairing rather than escalating: Saudi Arabia says the East-West pipeline can restart within days after the Iran-affiliated strikes that suspended it, Aramco expects to restore half of daily flows, satellite data shows 2.8m bpd moving through Hormuz over six days versus 700k bpd in August, and WTI fell 2.34% to $99.53 on Friday with Brent at $103.21. A decaying catalyst gets a smaller position, so 14% -> 10%. I am not cutting it to zero for two reasons: Hormuz transit is still materially disrupted and any re-escalation is a fast, large upside gap that nothing else in this book participates in, and $100 crude mechanically flows into US energy Q3 results in late October, which is the next hard-dated catalyst this leg owns. Take-profit tightened from 20% to 15% because the easy part of the move has happened; stop stays wide at 12% because the whole point of the leg is to survive the chop and be there for the tail.

This is the one post-earnings-drift leg where the revision test still passes on fresh evidence rather than on memory: nine upward current-year EPS estimate revisions over the last 30 days against zero cuts, with Mizuho lifting its target to $215 from $175 and Citi to $225 from $170, against a ~$192 mark. Drift works when the estimate tape keeps moving in the direction of the surprise, and it is. I am adding 6% -> 9% precisely because it now carries the drift sleeve alone after CRM was cut - CRM failed the identical test in the opposite direction, falling on a guidance raise and again into its own user conference, which is what an exhausted drift looks like. Sizing stays modest because this is high-multiple software going into a Fed that just hiked with the 10-year above 5%. Take-profit 9% keeps the discipline of harvesting drift rather than marrying the name; 10% stop.

A deliberately small hedge, not a macro call. The 2026-09-16 FOMC hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00% - the first hike in three years - unanimously, with 16 of 18 participants projecting at least one further hike in 2026 and Warsh emphasising persistent inflation, and the 10-year is back above 5%. That is a poor setting for multiple expansion, and stocks have already erased the hawkish reaction on nothing more than a one-day retreat in oil and yields. I hold 19% of genuine long beta (XLE plus TEAM); a 6% short covers roughly a third of it, which is the right ratio for a book whose job is idiosyncratic events rather than direction. Trimmed 8% -> 6% because the long beta it hedges shrank by more. Short borrow costs 3% APR, so I keep it small and stopped at 7% - if the market is squeezing higher against a hiking Fed, I want to be told to stop paying for the hedge rather than to keep financing it.

decisions.reason: Last week's book was built on one macro bet: that the 2026-09-16 hike was fully priced, so rate-sensitive and beta washouts would revert once the event passed. The event passed and the bet was wrong in the direction that matters. The Fed took the range to 3.75-4.00% and the 10-year did not fall - it touched 5.02% and closed above 5% on Friday as oil-driven term premium rebuilt. 'The Fed is priced' is therefore no longer a reason to own rate-sensitives; it is a reason to stop owning them. Applying my own rule (buy oversold quality whose drawdown cause is priced or resolving, refuse oversold whose cause is live and unpriced) honestly to the 2026-09-18 tape cuts three legs. HD goes because its cause is live and worsening, not priced: mortgage rates at a one-year high, the 10-year through 5%, and management on record that housing turnover has never been lower as a share of stock with 'no sign of an inflection point'. SYK goes because its drawdown is company-specific and unresolved - the cyber-incident supply drag is still costing 70-80bps of growth and management guides it into Q4, and Canaccord cut its target to $385 on 9/17; it is my worst leg for a reason, not by accident. The DELL short goes because the fundamentals moved hard against it: record $60.9bn of AI server orders, a $95bn backlog, and FY guidance raised to $192bn revenue. Shorting 'crowded' is a valuation opinion; shorting a company whose EPS just tripled is a fight, and mean reversion is not a licence to fight a confirmed fundamental upgrade. What I redeploy into is not new risk appetite, it is better-evidenced reversion. SNPS is the single best setup on my screen and gets sized up rather than trimmed: at $384.97 it sits 29% below its 52-week high and within 6% of its 52-week low, yet it raised annual guidance, beat on Q3 at $2.477bn revenue, and carries a $546 consensus target - the AI-pacing shock hit it by association, but EDA is a royalty on design starts, not on hyperscaler capex, so the sell-off is transmission, not damage. DAL is the one genuinely new idea and it is the cleanest expression of the discipline: the cause of its 17% drawdown is jet fuel, and jet fuel is actively reversing as WTI fell ~4% in two sessions toward $101 on Saudi Arabia restoring half the East-West pipeline within days. I have deliberately kept the defense block alongside it, because DAL and LMT/GD form a natural hedge across the one variable I cannot forecast: Hormuz. If the strait re-escalates, oil and defense rise and DAL is the loser; if it de-escalates, DAL is the winner and defense gives back its option value. That is intentional, not an accident of construction. Gross exposure comes down from 84% to 78% and cash rises from 16% to 22%, because a first hiking cycle since 2023 with a 5% long bond and an unresolved oil supply shock is a genuine reason to hold dry powder rather than a reason to be fully invested in reversion.
decisions.strategy: Concentrated long book of oversold US large-cap quality whose drawdown cause is now priced or actively reversing (EDA near 52-week lows with raised guidance, defense at a 23% discount into a rising budget, an airline as jet fuel rolls over), with every leg whose drawdown cause is still live and worsening cut, and 22% cash held at 4% against a 10-year yield back above 5%.

positions.thesis: Largest weight because it is the widest gap I can find between price action and fundamental direction. At $384.97 SNPS is 29% below its 52-week high of $539.48 and only ~6% above its 52-week low of $362.55, i.e. it is priced as if something broke - but Q3 revenue came in above guidance at $2.477bn with $2.84 diluted EPS on Design Automation strength, and the company RAISED annual forecasts, with 25 analysts at Strong Buy and a $546 average target. The drawdown cause is the AI-capex pacing shock that hit the whole complex when Alphabet took 2026 capex to $195-205bn against shrinking free cash flow; that shock is a real problem for names whose revenue is hyperscaler capex, but EDA licences are a toll on chip design starts, which are set by product roadmaps years ahead of any single year's datacenter budget. The stock was sold for a cause that does not touch its income statement, and that is the exact definition of my mandate. The 68x PE is why the stop is 16% rather than tighter - a rich multiple falling from a low base can still fall further - but the reversion target of 24% still sits well inside the consensus target.

Sized up from 10% to 15% because this is the rare case where the stock is deeply oversold and the fundamental cause is not merely priced but actively improving. LMT at $533.38 is 23% below its 52-week high of $692.00 on a 19.7x PE with a 2.59% yield, a valuation discount to every major peer. Against that, in the days around the poll: UBS upgraded to Buy on missiles and munitions growth, the administration approved a $24.3bn sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, Germany rolled out its first domestically produced F-35A, and the company took an $871m Navy modification plus a $1.21bn Army precision-strike missile award - on top of a backlog above $160bn and an FY2027 request calling for a step up toward $1.5tn of total defense spend. The de-rating was a 2026 margin and program-charge story; the order book is telling the opposite story. It is also my hedge against the risk I cannot handicap: if Hormuz re-escalates and my airline leg is crushed, this is the leg that pays.

The one new name, and the purest form of the discipline: an oversold quality operator whose single drawdown cause is measurably reversing. DAL closed 2026-09-18 at $79.62, roughly 17% below its $95.68 52-week high, on a 13.2x PE, with sector RSI in the high 30s to low 40s. The entire drawdown is jet fuel - roughly +130% year on year, a $4bn incremental 2026 cost for Delta alone - and that input is now rolling over: WTI has shed almost 4% in two sessions toward $101 and Brent closed below $105 as Saudi Arabia restores about half of East-West pipeline capacity within days. Meanwhile the revenue side is intact: demand is described as very strong across the board, carriers expect to recover essentially all of the fuel increase through fares by Q4, and Rothschild raised its target to $105 the day before the poll. Sized at 11% rather than larger, and stopped at 15% rather than tighter, precisely because Hormuz is unresolved and a single tanker headline reverses the input - which is why the defense block sits opposite it.

Held at a slightly increased 10% as the diversifying half of the defense block. GD's revenue mix - Marine Systems shipbuilding, combat systems, and Gulfstream - is materially different from LMT's F-35-and-missiles concentration, so the pair captures the sector's valuation washout without doubling a single program risk. The FY26 baseline near $895bn plus Ukraine resupply and Indo-Pacific supplementals, and an FY27 request running far above it, are multi-year contracted demand that does not care about the 10-year at 5%, which matters in a book where I have just removed everything that does. The leg is down 1.93% since the 9/16 fill on no company news, which is drift rather than information, and Gulfstream's backlog gives an earnings kicker that pure primes lack.

Kept and nudged up to 9% as the low-beta anchor of the book. It is one of only two legs that is actually up since the 9/16 fill (+1.64%), which says the market is already re-rating it away from the AI-capex panic rather than toward it. Cisco sells networking and security into the same datacenter build that spooked everyone, but as an arms supplier with recurring software revenue and a dividend, not as a principal burning free cash flow to fund it - so the Alphabet/Oracle negative-FCF problem that drove the megacap complex down ~4.8% in a day is a customer-spend tailwind for Cisco, not a balance-sheet threat. Tight 11% stop and modest 14% target because this is a ballast position: its job is to hold value while SNPS and LMT do the work, not to double.

Held at 9%. Honeywell is the bridge between the two things this book now owns: aerospace and defense aftermarket on one side, industrial automation and energy-efficiency equipment on the other, with a portfolio separation that keeps a structural re-rating catalyst live independent of the macro. It is down only 0.58% since the fill, so the original oversold-industrial thesis has neither been confirmed nor broken in two sessions and there is no new information that justifies paying spread to exit. Unlike HD, which I am cutting, Honeywell's end demand is corporate and government capex under long-cycle contracts rather than US housing turnover, so a 5% 10-year does not sit directly on its revenue line.

Held at 8%, the smallest leg, because it is a genuine oversold-quality name but with a cause that is only partly resolved. At $942 it is 18% below its $1,153.99 52-week high on a 14.6x PE, and the proximate cause of the most recent 4% leg down was Solomon flagging softness in trading, with FICC guided slightly softer in Q3 against strong equities. That is a quarter-shaped problem, not a franchise problem, and a Fed that has just started hiking into a 5% long bond raises rate volatility, which is what FICC desks monetise once positioning resets. The honest caveat is that the FICC softness is still live and Q3 results land in mid-October, which is why this stays at 8% with a 13% stop rather than being sized as a conviction reversion leg.

decisions.reason: Two things changed. (1) The XLI/VTV leg failed my own filter and the macro turned against it. It never had a firm-specific catalyst - it was a cyclical-versus-defensive factor tilt dressed as a pair, exactly the construction I removed three of last week. The Hormuz supply shock now points it the wrong way: XLI carries roughly a fifth of its weight in transports and airlines facing $4.53/gal jet fuel and record diesel cracks (ULSD crack printed an all-time $108/bbl on 3 Sep), while VTV's energy sleeve is the direct beneficiary of $100-105 Brent. The tape agrees - transports and industrials are down five straight weeks and the pair has produced +0.34% of spread in three sessions on 32% of the book. Cut it. (2) I had the steel pair's catalyst half-wrong and checking it improved rather than weakened the thesis. Both names guided below consensus on 17 Sep, not just Nucor: STLD $5.34-5.38 vs ~$5.60, NUE $5.55-5.65 vs $5.99-6.17. The pair still worked (+~6% of spread in two days) because Nucor missed by roughly twice as much, and the reason is structural rather than a one-quarter print: Nucor guided its raw-materials segment DOWN, and that DRI/scrap complex is gas- and energy-intensive into an energy shock, while Steel Dynamics is getting metal-margin expansion FROM the same falling scrap cost, with record shipments and a backlog nearly 50% above last year extending through Q1 2027. Same HRC tape (~$1,200/ton, 50% Section 232, >1mt of Sep-Dec outages), opposite cost-side exposure. Keep it, do not upsize much - most of the headline repricing is already in the two-day move, and what remains is the slower cost-structure divergence into the ~20-21 Oct prints. The freed weight goes into a cleaner version of the same idea: on 16 Sep, at the same investor conference, in the same fuel environment, United RAISED full-year guidance to $9-11 while absorbing ~$6bn of incremental 2026 fuel, and American CUT to a -$0.65 to +$0.65 range with a Q3 adjusted LOSS of $0.10-0.70 despite 16-19% revenue growth. I am deliberately pairing against American rather than Delta: Delta's affirmation dates from 10 Jul and is stale, whereas United's is three days old. Gross stays at 60% and cash at 40% - both pairs are now correlated to the same war/fuel axis in their second order, and a US-Iran de-escalation headline is the live way this book loses, so I am not levering it up.
decisions.strategy: Two equal-weighted, same-industry relative-value pairs (STLD/NUE in steel, UAL/AAL in network airlines), each built on a dated company-specific guidance divergence from the week of 2026-09-16, run at 60% gross with 40% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Long leg of the steel pair, resized 13->15 because the 17 Sep guidance made the relative case stronger, not weaker. STLD guided Q3 to $5.34-5.38 against $3.69 sequentially and $2.74 a year ago - a ~45% sequential jump - on metal-margin expansion across the platform, record shipments, and the combination of higher realized selling values with LOWER scrap cost. The backlog is nearly 50% above prior-year and extends through Q1 2027 on commercial construction, data centers, manufacturing and healthcare, so the order book is not a spot-price bet. It still guided under a ~$5.60 consensus and the stock is -1.25% from my 16 Sep fill, which is the point: I am paid the difference between a modest miss and a large one, not the absolute print. Held long into the ~21 Oct report against a short in the name with the worse cost trajectory.

Short leg of the steel pair, equal-weighted to STLD to keep it dollar-neutral and isolate the cost-structure divergence. Nucor guided Q3 to $5.55-5.65 against $5.99-6.17 consensus - roughly a 7-9% miss versus STLD's ~4% - and shares fell 3.7% after hours on 17 Sep, +4.72% for me already. What keeps me short rather than taking the money is the composition: Nucor explicitly guided the raw materials segment DOWN while steel mills improve, and that segment is its energy-intensive DRI and scrap operation, which gets worse as the Hormuz shock feeds through industrial energy costs - whereas the same falling scrap price is what is expanding Steel Dynamics' metal margin. Nucor also bought back ~2.03m shares at an average $247.04 in Q3, above the current $248.38 mark, so the buyback is no longer accretive support at these levels. Same HRC price, same tariffs, opposite input exposure. 15% stop, wider than the prior 12%, because an HRC squeeze from the Sep-Dec outages would lift both legs and I do not want the hedge broken by a sector-wide rally.

Long leg of the new airline pair. On 16 Sep United RAISED full-year guidance to $9-11 per share while simultaneously disclosing nearly $6bn of additional 2026 fuel expense versus its start-of-year assumption and ~$575m of incremental Q3 fuel cost - i.e. it absorbed the entire Hormuz fuel shock and still guided higher, which is a direct demonstration that its premium cabin and loyalty revenue mix carries pricing power the industry as a whole does not have. It is trimming some December flights alongside the rest of the industry, so the capacity discipline that supports fares cuts in its favour too. Sized equal to the AAL short so the pair is dollar-neutral and the sector-wide fuel level is hedged out at first order; what is left is the quality spread. 15% stop as disaster protection only.

Short leg of the airline pair, and the position with the clearest forward asymmetry in this book. On the same day and at the same conference where United raised, American CUT full-year guidance to a -$0.65 to +$0.65 adjusted range from -$0.40 to +$1.10, and guided Q3 to an adjusted LOSS of $0.10-0.70 despite 16-19% revenue growth - a loss on strong revenue is an operating-leverage and cost problem, not a demand problem. Two details make the cut look incomplete: the Q3 guide assumes $3.75/gal fuel while jet fuel printed $4.53/gal on 17 Sep, about 17% above the assumption, and management separately said the latest increase adds roughly $1bn to Q4 costs. With the sector's most leveraged balance sheet, American's equity is effectively a levered claim on a margin that has just gone negative, so a second downgrade into the ~23 Oct print is the base case. The honest risk is that this is the most crowded short in the group and a US-Iran de-escalation headline would rip it, which is why the stop is 20% rather than tight - a noise-level squeeze should not close the position, but a regime change should. Note the leg is charged 12bps per side as a sub-$15 stock plus 3% borrow, which the expected spread comfortably covers.

decisions.reason: This book exists to be short the market's worst four calendar weeks, and the single worst week in that window is the one that starts on my entry date. The leg I would be replacing filled only three sessions ago (2026-09-16) and the seasonal event it was built for has not happened yet: the week after September quarterly opex is down 27 of 34 years since 1990, average -1.06%, with only four meaningful up-years (1998, 2001, 2010, 2016). Selling the position I built for that week on the Monday the week begins is the exact behaviour the calendar discipline is supposed to prevent. Nothing since Wednesday breaks the thesis; if anything the catalyst got stronger. The FOMC delivered the 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00% on a 12-0 vote and 16 of 18 dots show at least one more hike this year with the path extending into 2027, so short IEF (18%) and short XLU (7%), the two legs that need higher-for-longer intermediate rates, are running into a Fed that just told the market it is not done, with the 10y still at 4.96% and pressing 5%. Friday's 5bp yield dip and 1.7% Nasdaq bounce are a relief trade off an oil headline, not a regime change, and both of my short legs are effectively flat through it, which is what a low-gross seasonal book should look like mid-window. On the long side XLF (12%) is the rate-structure beneficiary and the pre-positioned entry into the midterm-year Q4 rally, XLE (9%) still has a live catalyst since Strait of Hormuz traffic remains largely restricted even with the Saudi East-West pipeline restarting, and GLD (8%) is doing its job as the hedge at +2.41%, the only leg with a real cushion. I checked the one exogenous event that would have justified a mid-window change, the Oct-1 funding cliff, and it is gone: the CR was signed 2026-09-02 funding through Dec 11, so the classic late-September fiscal tail risk is off the table and there is no reason to add gross defensively either. That leaves 54% gross and 46% cash exactly where the strategy of record wants them, because the 46% is not idle, it is pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 rotation into the midterm-year Q4 rally off the autumn low, earning 4% while it waits. The only tweak I seriously considered was trimming XLE as Brent eases from $106 to ~$99.5 toward the EIA's $90 2H26 path, but the engine gives me no way to resize one 9% leg: I would have to tear down and refill all five, paying 2bps a side on roughly 108% of turnover plus SEC/TAF, and, worse, resetting every stop and take-profit anchor to a new Monday fill, which would throw away the GLD cushion and re-risk four legs that are working, all to express a marginal view on my smallest-but-one position. That trade is not worth it. Hold the book, let the worst week of the year run against the positions it was designed for, and spend the churn budget on the Oct-1 rotation instead.

No regime change, a rank refresh. Three things moved in the two sessions since my 2026-09-16 fill. (1) The 9/16 FOMC delivered the first hike since 2023 to 3.75-4.00% on a 12-0 vote, 16 of 18 dots show at least one more, and the 10y sits near 5% - the bond bear trend that is the spine of this book got confirmed, not faded, so I add to the TLT short. (2) Crude reversed hard: Brent printed above 109 on the Saudi pipeline/Houthi strikes Tuesday and then fell three straight sessions to ~103.70, WTI ~101, as the market decided the export disruption is smaller and shorter than feared. My USO leg is the only losing leg and the momentum rank of spot crude has deteriorated from first to marginal - a trend follower cuts the leg whose signal is decaying rather than defending a thesis, so USO is halved to 7%. I keep a stub because crude is still above both moving averages with positive 3-month momentum; the signal weakened, it did not flip. (3) Gold made new highs near $4,400 on central-bank buying at 244t in Q1 and dollar debasement flows, and is my best leg at +2.41% in two days, so it takes the freed risk and becomes co-largest. XLE also takes some: energy equities are +28% YTD with sector EPS projected up ~57%, a cleaner and lower-vol expression of the same energy trend than a futures-roll vehicle. SPY is trimmed from 10% to 7% - it is still above both MAs, but it is the weakest-ranked of my longs and a Fed that is hiking into a 5% 10y is a headwind to the multiple, so it keeps its diversifying role at a smaller size. ITB short is untouched and is the leg I most want to own: mortgage rates back near 6.7%, new-home supply over nine months, buyer intentions down to 5.2% from 6.5% in a single month, DR Horton running a 20% cancellation rate and cutting FY26 revenue guidance. I deliberately do NOT add bitcoin despite it being the loudest tape in my packet (+26.6% against my -1.7%). BTC is ~$81k after a short squeeze, still far under the ~$126k October 2025 high, and well below its 200-day average - it fails my long screen. Chasing it would be abandoning the system to buy someone else's benchmark, which is the single fastest way for a trend book to die. Turnover here is ~20% of gross, a few cents of friction, not a churn of the book.
decisions.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across six asset classes with signals refreshed through the 2026-09-18 close: long where price is above both the 50- and 200-day moving average with positive 3-month momentum, short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility and then tilted toward the strongest-ranked signals - still the single 2026 macro trend of an energy/inflation shock into a hiking Fed, but with the tilt shifted out of spot crude and into gold and energy equities after this week's Saudi risk-premium unwind.

positions.thesis: Highest-conviction and lowest-volatility trend in the book, so inverse-vol sizing puts it at the top. TLT is below its 50- and 200-day averages with negative 3-month momentum and the policy path just hardened underneath it: a 12-0 hike to 3.75-4.00%, a dot plot with 16 of 18 participants expecting more, year-end dots at 4.1-4.4%, and the 10y pinned near 5% with October hike odds rising. Short duration is the purest expression of the energy-shock-into-hiking-Fed regime. Sized up from 20% because the FOMC removed the main two-sided risk to it. Stop 10% on a 20-year bond ETF is roughly a 2.5-sigma move in yields and would mean the trend has genuinely broken.

Strongest-ranked signal in the book and the one leg making new highs, so the tilt rule sends it the risk I take out of crude. Gold is at records near $4,400, above both moving averages with the best 3-month momentum of anything on my screen, and the bid is structural rather than positional: central banks bought 244 tonnes in Q1 at the fastest pace in years, diversifying away from dollar assets on fiscal and Fed-independence concerns. It is also the one long that does not need the energy shock to persist - it works on dollar debasement, on the inflation the Fed is hiking against, and on any risk-off that would hurt my SPY and XLE legs. Raised from 16% to 22%. Stop widened to 12% to respect elevated realised vol at these levels without giving up the trend to noise.

The energy trend is intact; I want to own it through producers rather than futures. XLE is up roughly 28-32% YTD against a near-flat SPY, holds well above both moving averages, and sector earnings are projected up ~57% for 2026 on high realised prices and strong refining margins, with Exxon and Chevron at 42.5% of the fund providing cash-flow ballast. Unlike USO it does not bleed on roll mechanics and it did not give back the whole Saudi spike this week - equities are discounting a multi-quarter price level, not Tuesday's headline. Raised from 18% to 20% as the preferred energy vehicle. Wide 18% stop because this is my highest-beta long and I do not want a normal commodity-equity drawdown to stop me out of the year's best sector trend.

Halved from 14% because the signal is decaying, not because the thesis is dead. Brent spiked over 109 on the Saudi pipeline attacks and has fallen three consecutive sessions to ~103.70 with WTI ~101 as the market priced a faster export restart - a disruption premium unwinding, which is exactly the pattern a time-series model should fade rather than average into. It stays in the book at a stub weight because crude is still above both moving averages with positive 3-month momentum and the physical market is not normal: October Fujairah-Asia supertanker rates are at record highs. At 7% a full stop-out costs the book about one percent of NAV, which is the right price for optionality on the next Middle East headline. Take-profit at 35% left on to harvest any genuine re-escalation spike.

Unchanged at 12% and the cleanest short in the book after TLT. Homebuilders are below both moving averages with negative 3-month momentum, ITB is down ~2% YTD while the index is up double digits, and the fundamentals are deteriorating in the direction the trend is already pointing: mortgage rates back near 6.7% and rising with the 10y at 5%, over nine months of new-home supply, buying intentions collapsing to 5.2% from 6.5% in one month - the largest monthly drop in five years - and DR Horton, 15% of the fund, posting a 20% cancellation rate and cutting FY26 revenue guidance to $32.5-33bn. This is the second-order expression of the same rate trend as the TLT short, but on an asset where the operating leverage runs against the owner. Checked REITs as a companion short and rejected it - real estate is outperforming in 2026, so the weakness is specific to for-sale housing.

Trimmed from 10% to 7%. The signal is still valid - SPY is above both moving averages with positive 3-month momentum and closed the post-FOMC week almost unchanged at 7,650, absorbing the first hike in three years without breaking - so the system keeps it. But it is the weakest-ranked of my longs and it now carries an identifiable regime headwind: a Fed that has committed to fighting inflation with more hikes into a 5% 10y compresses multiples even when earnings hold. Its job here is to diversify a book that is otherwise long inflation and short duration, and it can do that at a smaller size. Tighter 10% stop than my commodity legs because if the equity trend breaks in a hiking cycle it tends to break fast and I would rather be out and hold the cash at 4%.

decisions.reason: Three things changed since the 16 Sep fill. (1) The reason for my 22% cash is gone: the FOMC delivered the 91%-priced 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote, the S&P closed the week flat (-0.1%), and the event risk I was paid to avoid has passed. Holding a fifth of the book at 4% APY while my highest-conviction thesis runs at maximum intensity is now an unfunded underweight, so I redeploy to 14% cash and 86% gross. (2) The tape separated crude beta from refining margin, and I am paid for the margin, not the barrel. Brent fell three straight sessions to $103 as Saudi loadings rerouted through Oman, and EIA's September STEO still forecasts Brent averaging ~$90 in 2H26 - yet MPC/VLO/PSX rose 2.5-3.2% into that decline, because cracks widen when feedstock falls and products do not. XLE, which is 40%+ XOM/CVX crude beta, returned +0.44% over the same three days and is the leg the tape told me to cut. Brent's 2026 path ($118 in March, $70 by 1 July, back above $100 in late July, $87-97 in August, $103-109 now) is a whipsaw I do not want directional exposure to; the refining shortage has been one-directional because it is physical, not speculative: US refinery utilisation 97.8%, distillate stocks 13% below the five-year average, an Aramco refinery hit, and the 7 mb/d East-West pipeline shut on 11 Sep. Diesel cracks closed at a record $107.72/bbl on 10 Sep. (3) The main bear case is weaker than it looks. The obvious killer of this trade is an Iran ceasefire deflating the risk premium - but a US-Iran ceasefire was already announced on 8 April 2026 and Hormuz traffic never recovered, with tankers still burning this week. The market has already learned that a headline does not restore flows, so the ceasefire tail is partly spent. I therefore rotate XLE's crude beta into the same theme one link further down the chain: PBF for maximum crack torque and STNG for the ton-mile consequence of the pipeline closure. Stops are tightened to 12-14% across the book because every long now shares one factor and I want the disaster exit closer.
decisions.strategy: Own the physical refining-and-logistics margin of the Iran-war fuel crisis at 69% gross long (four refiners plus product tankers), cut the diluted crude-beta ETF, and keep 17% short the two most direct victims of $4.71 jet fuel and a hiking Fed, with the FOMC cash buffer now redeployed.

positions.thesis: Largest US refiner at ~3 mb/d with the heaviest distillate yield of the majors, which is exactly where the shortage is: distillate stocks 13% below the five-year average and the diesel crack at a record $107.72/bbl on 10 Sep. Marked +2.65% since the 16 Sep fill while crude fell three sessions, confirming margin capture rather than barrel beta. MPLX midstream cash flow funds the buyback through the cycle, so I am paid to wait for the late-October Q3 print, which on current cracks will be a blowout. Raised from 18% to 20% as the largest single leg because it pairs the theme's highest quality with the theme's highest conviction.

The purest refining pure-play in the book - no midstream, no chemicals, so the highest beta per dollar to the crack spread itself. Its Gulf Coast complex is the swing exporter into the Atlantic Basin, where the IEA now describes margins as at record levels, so VLO monetises the arbitrage that the East-West pipeline closure and Hormuz reroutings created. Up 2.48% in three sessions and part of the four-refiner group that has now risen six consecutive weeks. Raised from 16% to 18% with cash from XLE because I want the pure margin, not the diluted index.

Best leg of the three on the 16 Sep entry at +3.21%, and the most diversified: refining plus midstream plus the CPChem stake, which gives a cash-flow floor if cracks mean-revert faster than I expect. That optionality is why it stays a third-sized position rather than a headline one - it is the hedged expression within the refining sleeve. Nudged 9% to 10% to keep the sleeve balanced after XLE came out.

New. The highest-torque listed expression of the crack spread: small-cap, un-hedged, structurally levered to margin, trading at $77.19 with a forward P/E of 3.74 after Q2 adjusted EPS of $6.22 beat consensus, and it just termed out liquidity with $500m of exchangeable notes on 14 Sep. Deliberately sized at only 7% because it is the crowded-momentum leg: market cap is up 160% and the average analyst target of $72.54 sits below spot with Morgan Stanley at Underweight, so the sell side thinks it is finished. I want the convexity, not the concentration, hence the smallest weight and the tightest stop in the book.

New, and the highest-value idea this week: the same shortage one link down the chain, at a fraction of the multiple. Shutting the 7 mb/d East-West pipeline does not destroy barrels, it lengthens their voyage - more than 4 mb/d of export capacity is forced back toward Hormuz and Saudi crude is now loading via Oman, while the record Atlantic Basin diesel arb pulls product cargoes from the Gulf and Asia to Europe and the US. Both effects are pure ton-mile inflation for product tankers, and the war-risk premium is a second fare on top. The rates are already banked, not forecast: LR2 TCE averaged $64,900/day across 85% of Q3 revenue days and MRs $30,000/day, and management locked three-year charters at $40,188, $42,500 and $23,900/day - contracted cash flow that survives a ceasefire headline. Q2 net income of $243.7m against a $3.96bn market cap at a 5.4x P/E, with BTIG at $110 and a $95.90 street average versus $87.16 spot. Sized at 14% as the second-largest long because it is the only leg that is cheap, momentum-positive and diversifying within the theme.

Kept but trimmed from 10% to 8% - the one leg that went against me (-1.51%) while its fundamentals got worse, which is a warning I respect without abandoning. The case is brutal and still building: jet fuel at $4.53-4.71/gal on 17 Sep, near a 20-year high and more than double a year ago; American says the latest move alone adds ~$1bn to Q4 costs; Delta's adjusted fuel bill already rose 77% to $4.41bn; American, Southwest and Alaska have cut or withdrawn guidance, United is cancelling December departures and Southwest has halved 2026 capacity growth. This is the mirror image of my long: every dollar of distillate crack I collect at VLO and MPC is a dollar out of JETS' cost line. I trim rather than hold flat because capacity discipline lets survivors raise fares, and because the tape is discounting that offset faster than I expected.

The squeeze that the Fed just made worse. A 12-0 hike to 3.75-4.00% with 16 of 18 participants pencilling in another this year, into core PCE near 3.4% and headline revised to 3.7%, lands on a consumer already paying record pump and heating prices - a fuel tax and a rate tax at once, hitting equal-weight discretionary retail hardest because XRT's small-cap constituents have the thinnest margins and the most floating-rate debt. Working at +0.85% and raised from 10%'s share of a smaller book to 9% of a larger one. Kept at single digits rather than scaled up because the labour data stayed solid through the hike, which is the live argument against the consumer-rollover thesis.

decisions.reason: Three things changed since the 2026-09-16 fill. First, my own event-vol call came true and is now spent: VIX1D fell 22.9% to 13.12, VIX9D 23.1% to 13.39, VIX is 14.81 and index realized is 9.6% and falling, while VIX3M sits at 18.55 for a 3M/spot ratio of ~1.20-1.25 and the front VIX future trades 17.92, a 2.48-point premium to spot versus 0.79 the day before. I was holding long VIXY into exactly the configuration my own strategy of record said would crush it, and VIXY is -9.4% in a month and -49% in three. Owning it was internally incoherent; the coherent leg is the other side of the same roll. Second, the crude supply shock is being repaired: Brent is ~$103 from ~$109 at my fill, Aramco is restoring half of the East-West pipeline within days and full capacity in about six weeks, and Saudi is already pushing 2.8mbd through Hormuz against 700kbd in August. The asymmetric spike premium is half-spent and headline risk is now two-sided, so energy comes down from 40% gross to 28% and the pure spot-beta expression (XOP) goes entirely. Third, and this is the part that caps my short-vol size rather than expanding it: index vol is low because COR3M collapsed 11.4% to 11.58, not because components went quiet, while SKEW held at 145.70 straight through a 12.8% VIX drop. The crash bid never unwound. Implied correlation near 11 is a floor, and from a floor any macro shock re-correlates the index and gaps front vol. So I take the carry, which is genuinely at a multi-month extreme, in deliberately modest size behind a hard stop, and I hold 22% cash instead of buying the convexity back at a 2.48-point premium. Note for the record: the desk WebSearch budget was exhausted mid-research, so the last instrument check was done with WebFetch.
decisions.strategy: The post-FOMC vol crush I positioned for has happened, so the book stops paying for convexity and starts collecting it: flips the long VIXY leg to a short to harvest a front VIX futures premium of 2.48 points over a 14.81 spot with realized vol at 9.6% and falling, trims a crude supply shock whose physical cause is being repaired within days, and keeps short duration against a 5.00% 10y and a Fed signalling more hikes, with 22% cash at 4% as the tail hedge that steep contango makes too expensive to buy.

positions.thesis: The single largest carry in the listed vol complex right now, and the direct reversal of the leg I was wrong to hold. Front-month VIX futures at 17.92 against a 14.81 spot is a 2.48-point premium that has to decay into settlement unless spot rallies ~21%; against index realized of 9.6% and falling that is roughly a low-double-digit monthly roll, funded at 3% APR borrow. VIXY's own record confirms the mechanism rather than my forecast of it: -9.4% over one month, -49% over three, -96% over five years. Size is capped at 10% and not more precisely because my own regime read is bearish on its own tail: COR3M at 11.58 is near a floor and SKEW at 145.70 held flat through the whole vol unwind, so the crash bid is intact and a re-correlation event would gap this leg. A 25% stop caps a normal adverse move at about 2.5% of NAV; I accept gap risk beyond that as the price of the carry and refuse to size where a VIX print of 25 would be structural damage.

Highest-conviction directional leg and the one piece of the old book whose case strengthened rather than decayed. The 10y closed the week at 5.004% after the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00%, Warsh reaffirmed the inflation fight, the Fed has guided to at least one more hike this year and fed funds futures carry roughly 42% odds of two. Long duration is the wrong asset against an explicitly hawkish reaction function and a live crude-driven inflation impulse, and short borrow costs only 3% APR while the position is effectively long the same impulse my energy legs express. Sized up from 12% to 18% because it is the leg where the macro evidence moved my way. The 8% stop is set where a roughly 50bp rally in the 10y would say the higher-for-longer trade has broken, and a 15% take-profit marks where the move would be fully paid.

Kept as the core energy expression but trimmed from 20%, because crude is the one place volatility is still being realized and paid while the spot spike deflates. GVZ fell only 5.91% against a 12.8% VIX drop and OVX is near 50, so energy vol is holding while equity vol empties out; analysts still see sub-$100 Brent as unlikely with ~4mbd of routing at risk. XLE is the right vehicle for that now rather than E&P beta: the integrateds carry refining and marketing exposure that stays bid on tight product markets even as crude spot backs off from $109 to $103, so it decays more slowly than pure spot beta if the pipeline repair lands on schedule. The 13% stop is tightened from 15% because the asymmetry is narrower once the physical disruption is being fixed within days.

Held at roughly flat weight as the cleanest carry expression of a tight physical crude market. COMT holds the futures themselves, so it is paid the backwardation roll while the curve stays tight, which is exactly the part of the oil trade that survives the spot spike deflating: the pipeline can come back and the front of the curve can still pay to be owned. It also diversifies the energy sleeve away from equity beta at a moment when the index is quiet only because correlation cracked, and it is long the same inflation impulse as the TLT short, so the two legs reinforce rather than hedge each other. No take-profit: this is a carry position I want to keep collecting, not a spike I want to sell into.

The best-performing leg of the outgoing book at +1.61% and the right factor for this regime. With COR3M at 11.58 and DSPX up to 32.91, index-level moves are muted while components keep moving, which is the tape where a valuation factor earns its spread instead of being drowned by beta. Value is also the factor that holds up with the 10y at 5.00%, since a high discount rate penalises long-duration growth cash flows and leaves near-term earnings yield as what is actually being paid for. Held flat at 12% rather than pressed, because this is a factor tilt inside a vol mandate, not a stock-picking book.

Raised modestly from 8% as the low-beta ballast the book needs once I am net short volatility. If correlation re-couples from its 11.58 floor and index vol gaps, the VIXY short is the leg that hurts, and healthcare is the sector whose earnings stream is least geared to that shock and least geared to the crude impulse the rest of the book is long. It also carries no duration sensitivity worth the name against a 5% 10y, unlike the SPY and GDX beta I removed last week. This is deliberately a defensive allocation rather than a thesis about drug pipelines; the 10% stop reflects that I hold it for its low beta and would not keep it if it stopped behaving that way.

decisions.reason: The 9/16 FOMC resolved the question my week-9 book was built around, and the two sessions since told me my expression of it was wrong in one specific place. The Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote with 16 of 18 dots calling for at least one more, median 2026 PCE marked up to 3.7%, and the market now prices ~90% odds of another hike by December. The 10-year went through 5% for the first time since 2007 and finished the week near 4.998%, up over 2% on the week. The directional macro call embedded in my book -- inflation sticky, policy tightening, real assets over duration -- was confirmed. What was NOT confirmed is that broadening in this regime runs through small and mid caps. The week's tape was explicit: Russell 2000 fell and industrials and leveraged smaller firms lagged on refinancing and funding-cost pressure, while capital concentrated in balance-sheet-strong large caps and AI semis. Holding IWM, MDY, XLI and XLB at a combined 31% of gross into a tape that is punishing exactly the refinancing-vulnerable cohort is paying for beta that the funding-cost regime is actively taxing. So I keep the regime call and change the vehicle. Out: IWM and MDY entirely (highest refinancing sensitivity with front-end funding rising), XLB entirely (materials was my only losing long and a strengthening dollar plus a Saudi supply-normalisation narrative removes its catalyst), and XLI cut from 9 to 6. XLE cut from 20 to 14: WTI is still ~$96-100 and up nearly 19% on the month, but it fell three straight sessions as Saudi Aramco rerouted crude around the damaged East-West pipeline and signalled roughly half of capacity coming back, and Trump is publicly floating an end to the Iran war. Twenty percent in a leg with that much two-sided headline risk is a bet on the war, not on inflation. In: GDX raised 10 to 16 and a new GLD leg at 10. Gold at $4,418 is making highs INTO a strengthening dollar and a hiking Fed, which is the cleanest real-rate and fiscal-debasement tell available and the only leg in my book that actually made money. COWZ at 15 is the replacement for the small-cap sleeve: it buys broadening through cash-generative companies that fund themselves from operations rather than from a 5% credit market. The QQQ short comes down 6 to 4 -- I keep an anti-concentration hedge because a 5% ten-year eventually breaks long-duration equity, but I refuse to fund a large short against the one cohort the tape is rewarding. Churn cost is roughly 45% turnover at 2bps a side, under 2bps of NAV, which is cheap relative to carrying the wrong sleeve into more hikes.
decisions.strategy: Broadening re-expressed for a confirmed higher-for-longer tightening: an equal-weight core plus free-cash-flow value, a heavy hard-asset sleeve led by gold and gold miners, a trimmed energy weight as the war premium bleeds out, the refinancing-vulnerable small/mid-cap sleeve removed entirely, and a reduced anti-concentration QQQ short with an ETH debasement tail.

positions.thesis: The mandate anchor and the least-opinionated way to own participation beyond the top ten. Equal weight is up more than 6% since end-2025 against roughly 1.5% for the cap-weighted index, and index concentration in the top ten has fallen below 40%, so the multi-year broadening is intact even though RSP has lagged SPY since early August. At 18% it is the largest long: I am willing to sit through a narrowing patch in the core while I fix the leveraged tails around it, because RSP's constituents are S&P-quality large caps, not the refinancing-stressed small caps the week actually punished.

Raised from 10 to 16 and now the highest-conviction leg. Gold at $4,418 is advancing while the dollar strengthens and the Fed hikes, which is not how gold behaves on a normal rate impulse; it is how gold behaves when the market doubts that 3.7% PCE gets back to 2% without fiscal accommodation. Miners carry operating leverage to that: at a $4,400 gold price against all-in costs still set years ago, incremental revenue drops to free cash flow. It was my best leg at +2.89% in two sessions. The stop is wide at 20% because miner beta to bullion is roughly two-to-one and a 12% stop would be noise; the 40% take-profit reflects that this is the leg most likely to run rather than mean-revert.

New, and the direct replacement for the IWM and MDY sleeve I am cutting. My mandate is breadth, but the week's lesson is that breadth bought through small caps is really a short position in funding costs, and with the 10-year at 5% and the Fed signalling more, that trade loses on the financing line before the earnings line. COWZ screens the largest 1,000 US companies for free-cash-flow yield and weights by free cash flow, so it owns the non-mega-cap market through companies that self-fund. It is broadening with the leverage risk stripped out, which is precisely the distinction the tape drew between the Nasdaq's gain and the Russell's loss this week.

Trimmed from 20 to 14, still a core inflation leg. WTI near $96-100 is up roughly 19% on the month with Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab disruption still real, and integrateds are generating enormous free cash at these prices. But the marginal news has turned: crude fell three consecutive sessions as satellite data showed Saudi Arabia rerouting barrels around the damaged East-West pipeline with about half of capacity expected back, and Trump is signalling that an end to the Iran war may be near. That is a genuine two-sided risk and 20% was sizing the war rather than the inflation. Fourteen percent keeps the inflation hedge and the take-profit is cut to 30% because the easy part of the move is behind it.

New. I want the debasement exposure larger but not entirely through miner equity beta, which correlates with the broad market on risk-off days exactly when I need the hedge to work. Bullion at $4,418 gives the same real-rate and fiscal thesis with roughly half the volatility and no operational, jurisdictional or hedge-book risk, so GLD plus GDX at 26% combined is a sized real-asset core rather than a concentrated equity bet. The tight 12% stop is appropriate because if gold breaks down while the dollar is firming, my central premise that this is a debasement regime rather than an ordinary tightening is wrong and I want to be told early.

Cut from 9 to 6 rather than removed. Industrials were named among the week's laggards as higher borrowing costs pressured economically sensitive sectors, which is a real mark against the leg in the near term. I keep a reduced position because electrification, grid and reshoring capex are appropriations-funded and rate-insensitive on a multi-year view, and because zeroing every cyclical would leave the book a pure gold-and-energy trade rather than a breadth book. Six percent is the size at which being early costs me little.

Raised 2 to 3 and kept deliberately small. It is up 8.08% in two sessions and sits alongside gold as the second expression of the debasement tail, but on different plumbing: crypto rallied hard this cycle with BTC up nearly 27% over my book's life while my equity book went nowhere, so a token weight is the cheapest available option on that divergence persisting. Three percent is sized so a 25% drawdown costs 75bps of NAV, which is the most I will pay for a tail. Crypto spot at 35bps a side is the most expensive thing I trade, so I size it once and leave it alone.

Cut from 6 to 4 and kept only as a hedge. The strategic case is unchanged and arguably stronger: a 5% ten-year, the highest since 2007, is a brutal discount rate for the longest-duration equity in the market, and the Mag 7 are already down roughly 4% on average in 2026 with Microsoft off more than 17% on capex-without-revenue concerns. But the tactical evidence is against me right now -- the Nasdaq rose on the week while the Dow fell 1.7%, AI semis led, and this leg cost me 2.37% in two sessions. Halving it respects the tape without abandoning the thesis: at 4% it is anti-concentration insurance that costs little if I am early, and the 10% stop caps the damage if the narrowing runs further.

decisions.reason: This book is down 5.93% and I know exactly where the money went: the MTUM short, which cost 3.27% in two sessions, and unhedged currency exposure built on a dollar view that the FOMC just broke. Both are going. First, the dollar. My week-9 book rode emerging and international developed markets explicitly on a weakening dollar. The Fed then hiked to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote, marked 2026 PCE up to 3.7%, put 16 of 18 dots on at least one more hike with the 2027 median unchanged at 4.1%, and the market now prices roughly 90% odds of another hike by December. The ten-year went above 5% for the first time since 2007. The dollar strengthened into that as financial conditions tightened. A widening rate differential in the dollar's favour is the direct refutation of the premise VEA and EWJ were sized on, so I keep the assets and change the currency exposure: the Japan sleeve moves from EWJ to DXJ, which owns the same exporters with the yen hedged out, and unhedged broad developed is trimmed. Second, the momentum short. MTUM is the crowded US factor and shorting it was the whole anti-concentration expression in this book, but the week's tape ran the other way -- the Nasdaq rose while the Dow fell 1.7% and the Russell 2000 fell, with capital concentrating in durable-earnings large caps and AI semis. Fighting that with a 10% short while my longs were flat is paying tuition to be right later. I am not abandoning the view that this regime eventually breaks something expensive; I am moving the short to the instrument where the regime is already visibly working. Short TLT at 8%: long-duration Treasuries facing a 5% ten-year, 3.7% inflation and a committee that has restarted a hiking cycle is the cleanest short in the market right now, and it hedges my book against the one thing that would hurt every long I hold -- yields going higher still -- rather than against an equity factor that is currently winning. Third, ITA becomes EUAD. US defense at 12% was both my largest thematic bet and the one most exposed to a single headline, with Trump publicly saying an end to the Iran war may be near; European rearmament is a multi-year budgetary commitment that survives an Iran ceasefire, and it sits properly outside the US index-structure trade that my mandate is defined against. Fourth, VTV out and EFV in: US large-cap value is still the US cap-weighted complex wearing a value label, while international developed value gets me the same higher-for-longer factor tilt in cheaper, more financials-heavy markets. PAVE is cut entirely -- US infrastructure industrials were explicitly among the week's laggards on funding costs, and it was my weakest thematic justification. EWZ is new at 8: Brazil was named among the preferred carry-trade destinations this year, runs double-digit nominal policy rates that pay me to wait, and is a commodity exporter with oil near $96 and gold at $4,418. KIE is the one US leg I keep, because a 5% long end is a direct earnings upgrade for insurers' reinvestment books. Overlap with my Round 2 book is zero by symbol and by sector expression: Round 2 is US equal-weight, free-cash-flow value, gold and energy with a QQQ short; this book is international equity, European defense and a Treasury short.
decisions.strategy: Broadening owned entirely outside the US index-structure trade: emerging and international developed equity with the Japan sleeve currency-hedged against a firming dollar, European rather than US defense, international developed value, Brazil as the carry-and-commodity leg, insurance geared to a 5% long end, and the crowded-momentum short replaced by a short of long-duration Treasuries.

positions.thesis: Still the largest long despite the dollar turning against me, because EM's 2026 case no longer rests only on the currency. The MSCI EM index returned 34% in 2025 and is up roughly 7% this year, the asset class is being bought for carry rather than for beta, and EM central banks are largely ahead of the Fed in this cycle rather than behind it, so they own the real-rate advantage that used to belong to the US. It was my best leg at +1.60%. I hold the weight at 16 rather than raising it because a strengthening dollar is a genuine headwind to the translation math, and the 15% stop is the honest level at which I would concede that dollar strength has overwhelmed the local fundamentals.

Cut from 14 to 12 and kept unhedged deliberately. This is the Europe-weighted sleeve and the euro, unlike the yen, is not facing a central bank that is structurally behind the Fed; European rates have normalised and the ECB is not being forced into an emergency response to 3.7% US inflation. So the currency drag here is a fraction of what it is in Japan, and I would rather own the rerating of cheap European industrials and financials with the currency left alone than pay for a hedge I do not clearly need. The trim reflects that the dollar view underpinning my original 14% is no longer operative, not that the equity case has changed.

New, and it replaces EWJ one-for-one on the underlying while removing the currency. EWJ returned exactly nothing over my last leg, which is what an unhedged Japan position does when the equity market works and the yen does not. With the Fed restarting a hiking cycle and the BOJ still the most accommodative major central bank, the rate differential argues for further yen weakness -- and yen weakness is a direct earnings tailwind for the Japanese exporters this fund overweights, so hedging converts a drag into a compounding benefit. DXJ is the same thesis expressed so that the macro works for me twice instead of cancelling itself out. Size matches the conviction that Japan is the best-governed reflation story in developed markets.

Replaces ITA at the same weight and I regard the swap as a straight upgrade. My defense leg was sized on an active Iran war; Trump is now publicly saying an end may be near, and that headline would reprice US primes hard. European rearmament is a different animal: NATO commitments and national budget lines already legislated, procurement cycles measured in years, and order books that do not unwind because one Middle East conflict pauses. It is also a cleaner fit for a mandate defined as broadening outside the US index structure -- ITA is a US large-cap sector bet, EUAD is exposure I cannot get from any US index at all. The wide stop and 35% take-profit reflect a structural rerating rather than a trade.

Replaces VTV. The factor logic was always right -- a higher-for-longer curve favours value over growth because it compresses the terminal-value premium -- but VTV expressed it inside the US cap-weighted complex my mandate exists to avoid, and US value now trades at a premium to its own history. EFV gets the identical tilt in international developed markets at a materially lower multiple, with a heavier financials weight that is a direct beneficiary of a 5% long end rather than a victim of it. Nine percent is a factor tilt, not a thematic bet, and it is sized accordingly.

New. It is the one leg that benefits if oil stays high, which hedges the possibility that the Iran de-escalation I am fading in EUAD does not arrive. The 18% stop is wide because this is a high-volatility single country; 8% is the weight at which a full stop-out costs under 150bps of NAV.

Held at 8, the only US equity leg I keep. Insurers are the purest long-the-long-end equity: their float is reinvested at prevailing yields, so a ten-year at 5% -- the highest since 2007 -- mechanically raises investment income on every maturing bond for years, while hard-market pricing from catastrophe and war-risk losses supports the underwriting side at the same time. It marked down 1.07% in two sessions, which I read as noise in a rate-driven week rather than a thesis break. This is the leg that most directly monetises the same rate move my TLT short is shorting, so the two work together rather than against each other.

New, and it replaces the 10% MTUM short that was the single largest source of this book's drawdown. The case is the most direct one available: the Fed voted 12-0 to restart a hiking cycle, marked 2026 PCE up to 3.7%, put 16 of 18 dots on at least one more hike and holds the 2027 median at 4.1%, the market prices roughly 90% odds of another hike by December, and the ten-year has just broken 5% for the first time since 2007 and closed the week up over 2%. Long-duration Treasuries are the asset with the most to lose from every one of those facts and none of the offsetting earnings growth an equity short has to fight. It is also the correct hedge for this specific book -- rising yields are the common threat to EM, international developed and value alike -- whereas shorting momentum hedged me against a factor that is currently the market's leadership. The 10% stop sizes the risk at 80bps of NAV and would trigger only on a genuine growth-scare bid for duration, which is exactly the scenario in which I would want the short off.
