decisions.reason: This book's mandate is real-asset carry for a confirmed inflationary hiking regime, and on 2026-09-16 the regime stopped being a forecast and became a fact. The Fed raised the funds rate 25bp to 3.75-4.00%, unanimously, the first hike since 2023, and 16 of 18 participants now expect at least one more with four seeing two. CPI is 3.4% year-over-year, core PCE 3.3%, WTI is holding $95.71, gold closed at $4,418, the 10-year is at 4.998% and the 30-year at 19-year highs. That is, almost line for line, the world this book was built to own. It would be perverse to tear it up three sessions after the thesis was confirmed. The marks agree: SLV +5.05%, GDX +2.89%, AMGN +2.47%, GLD +2.41%, GILD +1.65%, VLUE +1.61%, MRK +1.35%, XLE +0.44% since the 9/16 fill, with only COMT (-0.69%), USMV (-0.10%) and VTIP (-0.08%) marginally red. The book is +1.45% lifetime on a max drawdown of 3.13% - low-beta carry behaving exactly as low-beta carry should. The VTIP anchor is the leg I scrutinised hardest and it is the leg most vindicated: while short-dated TIPS sit flat at 49.31 with essentially no duration damage, TLT closed at $81.25 against a 52-week low of $80.46 and is -5.71% over one year. Holding the inflation accrual with almost no duration is precisely the right place to be with the curve repricing toward 5%, and swapping it for anything longer would be buying the one asset the hiking cycle is actively destroying. The decision to strip the short-volatility and credit-beta sleeves ahead of the FOMC also proved right - the week's tape showed investors buying only durable-earnings mega-cap tech while industrials, cyclicals and small caps were sold, which is the kind of narrow, defensive breadth in which credit beta and short vol are the first things to break. The one genuine criticism I can level is the 23% combined in XLE and COMT: energy equities were among September's weakest sectors even with crude above $95, a divergence between the commodity and the equities that I am watching. But XLE is green since entry, its 13% stop is live and would take me out if the divergence resolves downward, and COMT holds the commodities themselves rather than the equities, so it is exposed to the price that is actually holding up. That is a leg to monitor, not a reason to pay two sides of friction on an entire $1,000 book. Churn is the real argument here. A full replacement costs about 2bps per side across every leg plus the SEC/TAF on the sells, and it would buy back most of the same exposure under different tickers - paying real basis points to end up in the same regime trade. Idle cash at 13% is already earning 4% APY, which in a hiking cycle is a paying position rather than a drag. Nothing in this week's tape contradicts a single leg, so the correct action is none. Noting for the record that this keeps the Round 3 novelty rule comfortably satisfied: my Round 2 book for 2026-09-21 is semiconductors, memory, E&P energy and short Treasuries and small caps - SMH, MU, AVGO, AMAT, XOP long, TLT and IWM short - which shares zero symbols and zero same-direction gross weight with the eleven long real-asset and defensive legs held here.

Two things changed since the 09-16 leg went on. First, the thesis stopped being a hypothesis: on 09-18 alone SNDK +10.99%, LRCX +6.98%, STX +6.93%, WDC +4.13%, MU +3.92%, with NAND explicitly described as becoming central to AI infrastructure and data-center demand now dominating that market. My leg is up on all three memory names. Second, and more important, the valuations did not catch up with the prices: MU is at 7.02x forward against 22.92x trailing and SNDK at 8.37x against 24.29x, which is the market saying it does not believe these earnings persist for even one more year. That combination - confirmed tape, unconfirmed multiple - is the one setup where a book down 7.95% should be adding, not sitting at 32% cash earning 4%. So the cash comes down to 14%. I am also finally executing my own strategy of record, which said to cut the merchant-electron sleeve: VST is still in the book at 12% and is now $140.67 against a 52-week high of $219.82, sitting a hairsbreadth off its 52-week low of $132.66, with market cap down 33% - a broken name that a 5% ten-year keeps repricing as duration. It goes. In its place, one leg of LRCX: I checked STX as the alternative and it is 24x forward for the same AI-storage story, while LRCX at 30x forward is the only way to own the capex that MU, SNDK, Hynix and Samsung are about to spend out of these margins, with gross margins at a 20-year high and WFE spend being revised up. I am deliberately taking 86% gross into MU's 09-30 print at 7x forward, because a 7x multiple is what pays for that risk. Stops stay wide enough to survive an ordinary gap and tight enough to stop a thesis break.
decisions.strategy: All-in on the single cheapest bottleneck in the AI buildout - memory and storage bits at 7-8x forward earnings - sized up by cutting the 32% cash drag and the contradictory merchant-power leg, with one wafer-fab-equipment leg as the second-derivative claim on the capex those bit margins are about to fund.

positions.thesis: The single cheapest asset in the entire AI complex and therefore the correct largest position. MU trades at 7.02x forward earnings with trailing revenue +167% and net income +710.7%, meaning the market is pricing a near-total collapse of HBM and DRAM pricing inside twelve months. HBM is sold out on long-term agreements and conventional DRAM is being crowded out by HBM wafer conversion, so the supply side cannot deliver that collapse on that timeline. Earnings on 09-30 fall inside this holding window and are the explicit catalyst: at 7x forward, a print that merely confirms the current run-rate re-rates the multiple rather than the estimate. Sized at 34% - up from 26% - because conviction that is not expressed in size is not conviction, and this book is 7.95% behind with a thesis the tape has now confirmed. The 16% stop is the discipline: it is wide enough to absorb a normal post-print gap but it exits if the pricing cycle genuinely rolls over, which is the only thing that breaks this leg. 45% take-profit targets roughly 10x forward, still below the analyst consensus target of $1,513.

The purest NAND bit play and the second-cheapest thing I can find: 8.37x forward against 24.29x trailing, revenue +175.3% and $11.43B of net income on a $262B cap. The structural change is that NAND has stopped being a phone and laptop commodity and become AI-infrastructure inventory - data-center demand now dominates the market, which is exactly the demand profile that broke the old NAND cycle's amplitude. There is also a mechanical bid: confirmed S&P 100 inclusion forces index buying that is price-insensitive, which is why it printed +10.99% on 09-18. Sized at 26%, up from 16%, as the second leg of the concentrated bit thesis. The stop is deliberately the widest in the book at 22% because this is the highest-beta name I own - its 52-week range is $93.54 to $2,354.39 - and a 16% stop here would be noise, not risk management. 50% take-profit sits near the consensus $2,125 target.

Held flat at 14%, deliberately not increased, because it is the one leg where the numbers argue against me: WDC's forward PE of 21.97 is HIGHER than its trailing 18.18, which is consensus explicitly modelling an earnings decline - the opposite of what MU and SNDK's forward multiples say. I keep it rather than cut it because the nearline HDD story is real and separate from NAND: fiscal 2026 revenue $12.92B (+35.7%) with earnings +403.6%, and exabyte demand for cold AI storage is running ahead of a head-and-media supply base nobody has built capacity for in a decade. It is also the deepest value in the book on price - $441.36 against a 52-week high of $799.87, so a 45% drawdown already taken - against a consensus target of $664.92. But a leg whose own forward estimates disagree with its story earns a holding weight, not an adding weight. 18% stop reflects that lower conviction.

The literal picks-and-shovels leg, replacing VST. If MU and SNDK are earning at a 7-8x forward run-rate, that cash does not sit on the balance sheet - it becomes wafer fab equipment orders, and Lam is the memory-levered WFE vendor, with etch and deposition intensity rising structurally as DRAM goes to 3D and NAND stacks past 300 layers. The confirmation is already in the numbers rather than in a forecast: fiscal 2026 revenue $23.23B (+26%), earnings +35.6%, gross margins at a 20-year high, a 27% dividend raise and a $3B five-year R&D expansion - none of which a company does into a capex air pocket. It printed +6.98% on 09-18 alongside the memory names, which tells me the market is starting to price the same linkage. I sized it at only 12% and took STX over it only after checking: STX is 24x forward for the same AI-storage demand I already own twice, whereas LRCX at 30.30x forward is a different, later-cycle claim on the same bottleneck. 30x is outside my 7-21x cheap band, which is precisely why it is the smallest equity leg. It replaces VST because VST at $140.67 sits near its 52-week low of $132.66 with market cap down 33%, and my own strategy of record already said to cut that sleeve.

decisions.reason: This book is three sessions old, it is +13.67% against SPY's +2.73%, and the macro it was built for on 09-16 is precisely the macro that is live on 09-19. Every reason I would trade it is already inside it. Brent is above $100 and XLE is +47.38% year to date at $64.31 against a 52-week high of $66.17, with USO +105% over twelve months - the Saudi supply shock I built this around is not a forecast any more, it is the tape, and XLE, XOP and EWZ are all still within a percent of my 09-16 fills, so I am being offered the same entry I already have without paying the basis points again. The one piece of genuinely new information cuts both ways rather than one way: the marginal headline has turned to Saudi rerouting easing some crude supply fears, which is a reason to be careful about ADDING energy beta, not a reason to sell 36% of the book into a shock that is still unresolved. And the book was constructed so that this exact headline is hedged internally - GDX at 15% is the policy-mistake leg, and it is the leg the new data most favours: spot gold has rebounded to roughly $4,400 on central bank buying and SOFTER economic data, while GDX at $95.48 is still 18% below its 52-week high of $117.18, so the miners have not yet priced the metal. Crude easing while gold firms on soft data is the rotation this book already owns both sides of. The composition still reads correctly on valuation too: XOP at 11.48x is heavy in refiners (PBF, Delek, HF Sinclair), which widen cracks if crude backs off while product demand holds; EWZ at 9.80x with a 3.62% yield is a commodity exporter whose central bank is now cutting into easing inflation. Set against that, trading has a real, asymmetric cost I have already paid once this experiment: my Round 2 book is at leg 10 and is down 7.95%, and most of that damage came from re-deciding rather than from being wrong. Replacing this book also re-anchors five stop-losses at prices above my fills, which mechanically converts a three-day gain into a wider downside - I would be paying commission for the privilege of raising my own risk. The only cosmetic flaw is COPX carrying no take-profit, and at a 12% tail weight that is not worth a round trip to fix. Hold, let the stops do their job, and keep the decision budget for the point where crude actually resolves in one direction. Note on process: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I began, so all of the above was researched via WebFetch against live quote and news pages.

The 2026-09-16 FOMC delivered the outcome this book was not positioned for: a unanimous 25bp HIKE to 3.75-4.00%, the first since 2023, with the median year-end 2026 dot lifted to 4.10% from 3.80%. My week-9 book was designed INTO a live FOMC and filled at that same close, so its shape reflects a pre-decision view. The decision itself is new information and it changes the ranking inside my own defensive universe. The composition of the inflation matters more than the level: headline CPI is stuck at 3.4% with August MoM +0.4%, the hottest in three months, while core fell to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021. The Fed is therefore hiking against commodity and energy prices, not against services or wages, and it is doing so into an economy the statement calls solid with resilient spending and strong productivity. That combination - higher policy rates, solid growth, commodity-led headline inflation - is the single worst regime for bond-proxy defensives and a good one for cash-generative real-asset defensives. The tape agrees rather than merely theorizing: over twelve months XLE is +47.4% and XLV +24.9%, while XLP is +6.1% and XLU +0.2%, and on 9/18 XLP fell -0.83% into the post-hike session. So I am not changing mandate, I am reallocating inside it. Staples go to zero, the dividend sleeve is halved, and the proceeds go to healthcare, energy and the quality factor. This is a resize of roughly a quarter of the book at 2bps a side, well under two basis points of friction in total, not a churned full replacement - the legs I believe in keep their positions and their basis. Cash goes 22 to 20 rather than up, because 20% is already a real allocation now that the risk-free rate is 4% and rising, and I would rather own the healthcare discount than earn a fifth point of carry.
decisions.strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core concentrated in the two defensive sleeves that actually work against commodity-driven inflation and a hiking Fed - healthcare and high-free-cash-flow energy - with the quality and min-vol factor sleeves kept, the rate-sensitive bond-proxy sleeves cut hard (staples out entirely, dividend halved), and 20% cash held at a risk-free rate the Fed just raised.

positions.thesis: The mandate anchor, and the one large defensive sector whose defensiveness does not come from duration. Healthcare earnings are policy- and demographics-driven rather than discount-rate-driven, so a Fed moving to 4.00% and signalling 4.10% does not compress it the way it compresses staples and utilities. It is also working on the tape - +24.9% total return over twelve months - which separates it from the defensives that are cheap because they are broken. Concentration is 14.9% Eli Lilly and 10.6% Johnson & Johnson, so this is a large-cap pharma expression with real free cash flow, not a speculative one. Raised from 29 to 32 because if I am cutting rate-sensitive defensives I should fund the defensive that is not rate-sensitive rather than sit on the cash. A 12% stop on a 0.7-beta sector ETF is a wide enough leash to survive a normal drawdown and tight enough that a genuine regime break takes me out.

This is the leg the FOMC decision most directly argues for, so it gets raised from 12 to 16. The Fed is hiking because headline inflation is stuck at 3.4% on a +0.4% August print while core has fallen to 2.4% - that gap is energy and commodities. Owning the source of the inflation the central bank is fighting is a better hedge than owning gold against it, which is why this book moved out of gold, and with real yields at 2007 highs a non-yielding metal remains the worse expression. XLE is 20.1% Exxon and 15.2% Chevron at a 17x P/E and a 2.4% yield - integrated majors with genuine free-cash-flow cover, which is the quality half of my mandate, not a leveraged drilling bet. +47.4% over twelve months says the trend is intact. The 15% stop is wider than the rest of the book because energy carries more single-commodity volatility, and the 25% take-profit stays because this is a hedge with a target, not a permanent holding.

Raised from 9 to 14 because the quality factor is the most direct way to express what a hiking cycle actually does to companies. When the funds rate goes to 4.00% and the committee guides higher, the discriminator between firms is balance sheet and the ability to fund from internal cash rather than from the market. QUAL screens for high return on equity, low debt-to-equity and stable earnings growth, which is precisely that screen, and it does it across sectors rather than trapping me in one. It is the sleeve that lets me stay defensive without being long duration, which is the trap staples and utilities represent in this regime. It is also the only leg in this book that was positive on both marks since entry, at +0.83%, which is weak evidence but not evidence against. 12% stop consistent with the rest of the equity sleeve.

Min-vol is core to a low-beta mandate and I am keeping it, nudged from 8 to 10, but deliberately sized below the quality sleeve. The honest caveat is that minimum-variance optimisation naturally overweights the same rate-sensitive utilities and staples I am cutting elsewhere, so a larger USMV position would partly undo the reallocation I just made. At 10% it delivers the realised-volatility dampening the mandate requires - this book's max drawdown is -3.70% against an S&P that has been far choppier - without smuggling the bond-proxy exposure back in through the side door. The tighter 10% stop reflects that a min-vol fund breaking 10% would itself be the signal that the low-volatility regime assumption has failed.

Halved from 15 to 8 rather than cut to zero. The case against is real: a high-dividend screen is a duration screen in disguise, and with the risk-free rate at 4.00% and the dot plot pointing to 4.10%, cash competes directly with the yield that is SCHD's entire appeal - it has already marked -0.47% since entry while the book's non-yield legs marked positive. The case for keeping a residual is that SCHD's screen requires ten years of dividend growth plus free-cash-flow-to-debt and return-on-equity quality filters, so it is a cash-generation screen as much as a yield screen, and that half belongs in this mandate. 8% is the size at which it contributes income without making the book a leveraged bet against the Fed being done hiking. If the committee delivers the additional hike its own projections imply, this is the leg I cut next.

decisions.reason: Two things changed and they point the same way. First, and this is the leg that matters, the short SMH position is wrong and I am closing it. It was entered to express a broken AI-momentum trend; SMH is +88.3% over twelve months and rose 2.21% on 9/18 alone, and the leg is already -5.03% two marks after entry. A book whose mandate is trend stacking has no business being short the strongest measured trend in the investable universe - that was not a trend expression, it was a contrarian view wearing a trend book's clothes, and the tape has falsified it. I am closing it and I am deliberately NOT flipping it long. Reversing the exact ticker that just hurt me, after a +88% run and on a two-day loss, is whipsaw rather than discipline, and at 22.6% NVIDIA the residual risk in SMH is idiosyncratic rather than trend. Closing a broken leg and standing aside is a complete decision. Second, the 2026-09-16 FOMC hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00%, unanimously, with the year-end median dot lifted to 4.10% from 3.80%, into a statement describing solid activity, resilient spending and a stable unemployment rate. Headline CPI is stuck at 3.4% with a +0.4% August month, the hottest in three months, while core has fallen to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021 - so the Fed is tightening against commodities in a healthy economy. That is close to the ideal setting for every carry engine in this book: commodity carry is long the thing causing the problem, bank net-interest-margin is long the policy response, and managed-futures trend is long whichever of those keeps working. The SMH weight plus trims to the covered-call sleeve fund increases in commodity carry, financials carry and midstream. Gross exposure rises 84 to 88 and the book goes fully long-only, which I accept because the short I was carrying was the leg adding risk rather than reducing it. Turnover is roughly a third of the book at 2bps a side - under a basis point of friction to remove a position whose premise no longer exists.
decisions.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking with the falsified short-semiconductor leg closed and not reversed, weight pushed into the three carry engines a hiking Fed and commodity-led inflation actually pay - broad commodity carry, systematic managed-futures trend and bank net-interest-margin - alongside midstream and E&P energy carry and a reduced covered-call sleeve, all long-only.

positions.thesis: The single best carry-and-trend expression available right now and the book's largest leg, raised from 18 to 22. +51.7% total return over twelve months makes this the strongest non-semiconductor trend I can measure, and the macro confirms rather than contradicts the price: the Fed just hiked specifically because headline CPI will not fall below 3.4% while core has already dropped to 2.4%, and that entire wedge is commodities and energy. PDBC is actively managed to optimise roll yield rather than mechanically rolling front-month, so in a market where the carry is positive it harvests that carry instead of bleeding it, which is the difference between a commodity trend fund that compounds and one that does not. Being long the commodity complex is also the cleanest hedge against the risk that scares this book most - that the committee has to deliver more than the one further hike its own dots imply. 12% stop with a 25% target: this is a trend leg with a defined exit, not a permanent allocation.

Held flat at 20 and left untouched deliberately. This is systematic trend replication across futures markets and it has returned +25.8% over twelve months with a beta to equities of roughly -0.17, which is the property I am paying the 0.85% expense ratio for: it is the only leg that can make money if the equity and commodity legs around it break at the same time. It also solves the problem I created by closing the SMH short - with the book now long-only in cash equities, DBMF is the entire diversifier, and that argues for keeping it large rather than spending it on more directional carry. The honest risk is that its replication carries meaningful notional in 2-year and 10-year Treasury futures, and a Fed that keeps hiking past 4.10% would hurt that sleeve if it is positioned long duration. 20% is the size at which that risk is a drag rather than a wound, and the 12% stop bounds it.

Raised from 10 to 13 as the highest-quality carry leg in the energy complex. Midstream partnerships earn fee-based, volume-linked distributions on pipelines and terminals rather than taking direct commodity price risk, so this is a yield harvested from energy throughput rather than a bet on where crude prints - genuine carry, which is what this mandate is built around. It complements rather than duplicates the E&P exposure below: if energy prices chop sideways while volumes stay high, XOP goes nowhere and AMLP still pays. It also holds up better than other high-yield sleeves against the hike, because distribution coverage comes from contracted throughput with inflation escalators rather than from a fixed coupon that cash at 4.00% now competes with. 12% stop.

Raised from 8 to 12 because this is the leg the 9/16 decision most directly rewards, and it was underweight for a world that has now arrived. A unanimous hike to 3.75-4.00% with the median dot at 4.10% widens net interest margin on the asset side, and the statement's description of solid activity, resilient spending and a stable unemployment rate is exactly the credit backdrop that lets banks keep that margin rather than give it back in provisions. That combination - higher short rates plus benign credit - is the textbook setting for bank carry, and it is rare to get both. The risk is the inversion or credit-cycle scenario in which the Fed hikes into a slowdown, which is why this is 12% rather than the 20% the thesis might otherwise justify, and why it carries the same 12% stop as the rest of the book.

Trimmed from 12 to 11 and kept as the book's equity-volatility carry sleeve. Writing calls against a low-volatility equity portfolio monetises the implied-to-realised volatility spread, which is a real and persistent carry source and belongs in this mandate. The reason it is trimmed rather than raised is that the environment has shifted against the strategy's weak spot: with semiconductors running +88% on the year and the broad tape grinding higher post-hike, covered-call overlays cap exactly the upside participation that is being delivered, and the +0.55% mark since entry is consistent with that. It stays because the distribution stream is genuine and because it is the lowest-beta equity leg in the book, which matters more now that the short is gone. 10% stop, tighter than the rest, because a covered-call fund breaking 10% means the volatility regime itself has changed.

Held flat at 10 as the high-beta end of the energy trend. Equal-weighted E&P gives a more levered, more small-cap expression of the same commodity move PDBC captures at the index level and AMLP captures as throughput - if the energy trend that drove the sector +47% over the past year continues, this is where the convexity is. Held flat rather than raised because it is the most volatile leg in the book and because I am already adding to energy through AMLP; stacking a third increase on the same underlying driver would turn a diversified carry book into a one-factor energy fund. The -0.62% mark since entry is noise at this volatility. Widest stop in the book at 15% because equal-weighted E&P routinely draws down 10%+ inside an intact uptrend, paired with a 30% target that reflects the same asymmetry.

decisions.reason: What changed is the 2026-09-16 FOMC itself. I positioned last week for an inflation shock; the Fed then delivered its first rate HIKE since 2023, the 10-year pushed above 5% (highest since 2023), TLT printed 52-week lows and crude stayed elevated. That is not a marginal surprise, it is a discount-rate regime change, and it re-ranks my own book. Three specific re-rankings follow. (1) The discount rate now punishes duration inside equities, so yield-substitute staples lose their relative appeal: PEP's 4.56% yield no longer stands out against a 5% risk-free rate, it sits at a fresh 52-week low ($129.55 low vs $129.75 close), and the cited headwind is that high gasoline prices are cutting US consumer food spending, i.e. PEP is the direct cost of the energy long I am mandated to carry. I cut it 9 to 7 rather than to zero, because the contrarian mandate is to own capitulated quality, not to sell it at the low. (2) QCOM's 'cheap semis' premise broke on the news, not on the price: MediaTek claimed first-mover on 2nm, QCOM fell 5.8% on 09-18, and at 19.2x forward with a Hold consensus and only ~9% to target it is the most expensive value name I own. A de-rating that is competitive rather than cyclical is outside my mandate, so I halve it 11 to 6 instead of defending size. (3) The proceeds go to the legs where capitulation is reversing on evidence: ACN at 12.6x forward and a 3.6% yield, with the Anthropic and Google Cloud commitments and an ~8% move after the 09-18 close, is the mean-reversion actually firing; UNH at 17.7x forward with a $481 consensus target and CI alongside it are the cheapest quality cash flows I can buy and are largely insensitive to the 10-year. Energy weight is deliberately unchanged at 21% and not increased: XLE is up ~47% over a year and adding after that run would be momentum-chasing, which is not my strategy, but the hike makes cutting the hedge wrong too. Cash stays at 20% because a hiking Fed widens the distribution of outcomes and idle cash is now a paid option. Turnover is ~26% of gross, a few basis points, and that is a price worth paying to remove the two legs whose theses the week actually damaged.
decisions.strategy: Contrarian mean-reversion in capitulated quality/value, re-tilted for a confirmed rate-HIKE regime toward short-duration cash-flow value (managed care, cheap IT services, integrated energy) and away from bond-proxy staples and a semis name whose cheapness no longer holds, with the mandated inflation-shock hedge still expressed through cheap integrated energy, a small hard-asset crypto leg, and a 20% cash buffer earning 4%.

positions.thesis: Largest position because it is the cleanest expression of the mandate in a hiking world: a capitulated quality franchise ($376.90 against a 52-week range of $255.97-$461.62) at 17.7x forward earnings whose cash flows are essentially indifferent to a 5% 10-year. The 2025 earnings decline of 16% to $12.06bn on 11.9% revenue growth is a margin problem, which is cyclical and fixable, not a demand problem; management is attacking exactly that with AI claims processing and the removal of prior authorization on ~30% of procedures. 26 analysts at Buy with a $481.72 average target, ~28% above spot, means the sell side has not yet marked the recovery. Size up from 12% to 14% because it held green (+0.44%) through a week in which my rate-sensitive legs sold off, which is the relative-strength confirmation I want before adding to a value position.

The core of the mandated inflation-shock hedge, held flat at 13% rather than increased. A Fed that has just hiked into elevated crude and surging European gas prices is telling me the shock is real, and XOM at 13.2x forward with a 2.52% yield is still the cheap way to own it, with a possible Venezuela field re-entry as free optionality. I am explicitly not adding: XLE has returned ~47% over the past year and led August sectors at +7.4%, so incremental energy here is chasing a crowded trend rather than buying capitulation, and chasing is another strategy's job, not mine. 13% is the size that hedges the rest of the book without becoming the book. No take-profit, because within 8% of the 52-week high I want this leg to run if crude does; the 15% stop is the discipline if the shock reverses.

Raised from 10% to 12% because this is the mean-reversion thesis working in real time. At $181.29 the stock trades at 14.5x trailing and 12.6x forward with a 3.60% dividend yield, against a 52-week high of $291.09 -- a genuine capitulation in a quality franchise. The de-rating premise was that AI disintermediates consulting; the counter-evidence landed this week, with a partnership in which Accenture and Anthropic each commit at least $1bn over five years and a new Google Cloud business group, i.e. AI is arriving as a revenue line rather than a substitute. The stock moved roughly +8% after the 09-18 close on that news, so I am consciously paying up at the 09-21 fill rather than buying the low, and that is why I add only two points rather than doubling. Guggenheim's downgrade after the 52% bounce off June is the residual bear case and the reason the 15% stop stays. Q4 FY26 earnings on 01 October are the near-term catalyst that resolves it.

Raised from 7% to 10% as the second leg of the managed-care pair. The whole group was repriced for elevated medical-cost trend, and Cigna is the cheaper, less headline-exposed way to own the recovery than UNH alone; pairing them gives me sector conviction without single-name concentration in the one stock that carries the political and reputational risk. In a regime where the discount rate has just gone up, an insurer whose float actually earns more at 5% short rates is one of the few equity exposures that is helped rather than hurt by the hike. Down 1.84% on the week is noise, not thesis damage. 14% stop is set below the group's recent volatility band.

Held flat at 8% as the second integrated, diversifying the mandated energy hedge away from single-name Exxon risk while keeping total energy at 21% of the book. Chevron's balance sheet and dividend coverage make it the lower-beta half of the pair, which matters now that the Fed is tightening into the commodity shock rather than accommodating it -- the tail risk for energy is a hike-driven demand break, and in that scenario I would rather own the integrated with the cleaner balance sheet. Down 0.96% since the 09-16 fill is inside noise and changes nothing. No take-profit for the same reason as XOM; 15% stop is the exit if the demand-break tail arrives.

Cut from 9% to 7%, the deliberate compromise between mandate and macro. The macro case against: at a 4.56% dividend yield it is a yield substitute in a week when the risk-free rate moved above 5%, which removes its principal attraction, and the stated headwind -- high gasoline prices cutting US consumer food spending -- means my own energy long is the thing taxing this position. The mandate case for keeping it: at $129.75 it is sitting on its 52-week low of $129.55 at 14.9x forward, consensus $155 target, and selling a capitulated quality franchise at the exact low is how contrarian books turn drawdowns into permanent losses. So I reduce the size rather than the conviction and let the 12% stop, not my nerve, decide if it is a value trap.

Halved from 11% to 6% because the cheapness premise failed on evidence. At 19.2x forward with a Hold consensus and a $194.13 average target only ~9% above the $177.72 close, this is no longer a cheap semiconductor by any measure I would defend -- it is the most expensive earnings stream in a book whose whole point is buying discounted ones. The 5.82% drop on 09-18 came with MediaTek claiming first-mover advantage on 2nm smartphone silicon, which is a competitive share threat, and my mandate is cyclical de-ratings that mean-revert, not structural ones that do not. I keep a 6% residual rather than exiting because the $60bn Amazon custom AI datacenter chip agreement is a real, non-handset earnings stream the market is not yet paying for, and a 1.68 beta name at less than half of its $259.92 high has convex upside if that lands. Wide 18% stop is appropriate for the beta at this reduced size.

Held at 6%, the book's unlevered-enterprise-software sleeve and its most asymmetric single bet. Adobe carries the same market-imposed narrative as Accenture -- that generative AI destroys the incumbent -- and the Accenture news this week is the first hard evidence that enterprises buy AI through incumbents rather than around them. Only 0.63% below the 09-16 fill, so nothing in the price argues for changing size. I keep it deliberately small at 6% because I am not yet able to point to the same contractual proof for Adobe that I can for Accenture; the 40% take-profit against an 18% stop is the 2:1 payoff I am underwriting, and the position is sized so that being wrong costs roughly one percent of the book.

Held at 4% and not trimmed despite the hike. This was the oversold-crypto leg and it is now the book's best performer at +8.08% since 09-16 -- the mean-reversion premise has started to pay, and cutting a winner three days in to save 35bp of crypto commission is the wrong trade twice over. The macro logic also survives the hike: BTC is up 26.8% over the book's life against SPY's 1.7%, which says the market is treating scarce non-sovereign assets as an inflation expression rather than as a pure rate-sensitive risk asset, and that is the same shock my energy leg is hedging. I keep it at 4% rather than adding because a genuinely tightening Fed is a real headwind to liquidity-driven assets, so this stays position-sized as a diversifier. The 20% stop reflects the asset's volatility, not a lower conviction.

decisions.reason: This book is a quality-momentum/trend-following mandate, and the single question a trend book must answer each week is whether the trend it is riding was confirmed or broken. It was confirmed, emphatically, by the event that sits between my 09-16 fill and today. The Fed raised rates 25bp on 2026-09-16 -- its first hike since 2023 -- the 10-year yield pushed above 5% for the first time since 2023, TLT touched $80 on Monday for its lowest print since July 2025 against a 52-week range of $80.46-$92.19, crude stayed elevated, European natural gas prices are surging, and XLE has now returned roughly 47% over a year after topping the August sector table at +7.4%. Every one of those is the thesis of this book restated by the tape. Trading here would mean replacing positions whose reason for existing was just externally validated, which is the classic way a trend follower converts a working signal into transaction costs. The leg itself is three sessions old and net positive: VLO +2.48%, GDX +2.89%, XLE +0.44%, with XOP -0.62%, DBC -0.69%, XME -0.08%, XLF -0.13% and the TLT short -0.46% all inside two days of noise and none of them anywhere near their stops. There is no signal in that dispersion to act on; a 0.46% adverse mark on a short into a week when the Fed hiked is a pause in a trend, not a reversal, and TLT at the bottom of its 52-week range with a 5%-plus long end and freshly hawkish policy is exactly where a duration short should be held rather than covered. The one leg I genuinely examined for removal was XLF at 8%, since a hiking Fed can flatten or invert the curve and financials are owned here for steepening; I keep it because the hike came with a long end that rose faster than the front, which steepens rather than flattens, and because 8% is small enough that being early costs little. Against all of this, replacing the book would cost real basis points -- roughly 2bps per side across 80% gross plus SEC/TAF on the sells -- to buy back substantially the same exposure, and it would reset every stop-loss to a worse level, since my current stops sit under entry fills struck before this week's confirming move. Holding also preserves the sharp separation from my Round 2 value book, which carries no ETF or commodity exposure and no short at all, so same-direction gross-weight overlap between the two remains far below the 50% limit on any reading, symbol-level or economic. The book is aligned with the macro, hedged by hard stops under every leg and a 20% cash position earning 4%, and the correct action for a trend follower whose trend is intact is to leave it alone and let the winners run.
